title: Why Sunday can be day eight
question: Why can two people counting the same days disagree on the total?
hook: Count the days from one Sunday to the next and you may get seven or eight, depending on where you start.
idea: Counting a set is simple, but whether the starting point counts changes the total by one.

beats.prompt: A guest checks in on a Sunday and that Sunday counts as day 1 of the stay. Counting this way, which day number is the following Sunday?

choices.label: Day 7
choices.feedback: Tempting because a week has seven days, but the starting Sunday already took number one.

choices.label: Day 9
choices.feedback: This overshoots; the next Sunday is only one week after the start.

beats.explain: With inclusive counting the starting Sunday is day 1, so the following Sunday is the eighth day.

beats.prompt: match each counting method to what it suits
pairs: A small set counted over time
beats.explain: Each method has a setting where it is convenient: speaking suits what is in front of you, marks suit counting over time, and fingers suit small numbers.

beats.prompt: sort each example by how it counts
items: The French quinzaine for a fortnight, 15 days
The Roman nones, 8 days before the ides
Sunday is day 1, so the next Sunday is day 8
The English fortnight, from a fourteen-night
Eight days from Sunday, with Monday as day 1
beats.explain: Inclusive counting includes the starting point, as in Roman dates and the Romance languages. English counts exclusively.

beats.prompt: one step in this reasoning is wrong; which?
steps: Ana counts the starting day itself, so Sunday is day 1 for her.
Ben counts at the end of each interval, so his count skips the starting day.
Both count the same stretch of days, so their totals must come out equal.
So any difference between their totals must be an arithmetic slip.
beats.explain: Including or skipping the starting point changes the total: the inclusive count is always one greater for the same set.
